newsitem.title: ALBANIA: A rundown of Southern Albanian towns in rebel hands.
newsitem.headline: A rundown of Southern Albanian towns in rebel hands.

text.p: While Albanian President Sali Berisha and main opposition parties are trying to implement a political accord signed at the weekend, rebels continue to make big gains in southern regions, calling on Berisha to resign.

At least 10 major towns are in the hands of rebels refusing to hand in weapons in conformity with the agreement Berisha and ten political parties signed on Sunday. Here is the situation in southern Albania on Tuesday, according to reports from the area.

-- Vlore. Albania's second largest Adriatic port, effectively seized in early February by residents furious at the loss of their savings in the failed Gjallica pyramid investment scheme. The town of 80,000 came under control of more organised armed rebels on February 28 after confrontation between protesters and secret police.

-- Sarande. Smaller port and resort town further south, opposite the Greek holiday island of Corfu. Ferries regularly travel the short distance to the island. The town, with a population of about 15,000, is one of the centres for Albania's ethnic Greek community. It came under firm control of insurgents after Vlore.
-- Delvine. Sixteen km (10 miles) inland from Sarande. A small town which fell to the rebels in the same wave that brought the two ports under insurgent control.

-- Tepelene. A remote mountain town of 20,000 on the main national road south to Greece. It is the site of a top-security prison which held Socialist party leader Fatos Nano, jailed on corruption charges in 1994. He was moved to Tirana before the insurgents took control of the town last week and set up big artillery guns in the central square.
-- Memaliaj. A small town between Tepelene and Fieri, known as a coal area. The bridge over the Vjose river in the town has been blocked since last month, almost paralysing traffic in the south.

-- Gjirokaster. An ancient town and centre of the ethnic Greek community, only 30 km (20 miles) from the Greek border. Rebels overran the town and raided a big military barracks on Saturday after a government attempt to fly in troop reinforcements. President Berisha and the opposition have pointedly said the Greek community has no direct connection with the insurgents.

-- Permet. Town in one of Albania's most remote districts. Rebels who took control of it on Sunday before the political agreement was signed vowed not to surrender their weapons until Berisha resigned. Five people were killed and six injured in the fighting.

-- Berat. One of Albania's oldest towns, where rioting broke out in January over lost savings in pyramid schemes. Reports suggest that rebels tried to seize control of the town at the weekend. Hospital sources said one person had been killed and 20 slightly injured in random shooting, but there were no clashes.

-- Kucove. An oil refinery area, 18 km (11 miles) northeast of Berat where residents pillaged an air force base, one of two important military airfields in Albania. One person died after being hit by a stray bullet from celebratory fire. Kucove has been a stronghold of the main opposition Socialist Party.
-- Corovode. A remote town at the site of Tomorri mountain (2417 m), 50 km south of Berat. Corovode was earmarked by the late Stalinist leader Enver Hoxha as Albania's capital in case of war.
-- Polican. A small town between Corovode and Berat where there is a military plant producing Kalashnikov guns using Chinese technology.
-- Gramsh. This small town in central Albania, 96 km (58 miles) southeast of Tirana seems to be the latest to have fallen into rebel hands.
